questions.prompt: A cumulative frequency curve represents the examination scores of $160$ students. The curve passes through the point $(54, 112)$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State how many students scored at most $54$ marks, and find how many students scored more than $54$ marks.

questions.prompt: A cumulative frequency graph for $120$ battery lifetimes in hours passes through $(30, 28)$ and $(60, 94)$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the number of batteries with lifetimes between $30$ and $60$ hours, and express this count as a percentage of the total sample.

questions.prompt: A cumulative frequency distribution summarizes the masses of $200$ parcels.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the target cumulative frequencies used to estimate the lower quartile $Q_1$ and the upper quartile $Q_3$.

questions.prompt: From a cumulative frequency curve representing $80$ runners' race times, the lower quartile is read as $24.5\text{ minutes}$ and the upper quartile is read as $38.0\text{ minutes}$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the interquartile range (IQR), and interpret this value in words.

questions.prompt: A teacher wishes to estimate the 85th percentile of marks for a group of $240$ candidates from a cumulative frequency curve.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the target cumulative frequency required to locate the 85th percentile, and state whether the percentile is a mark value or a frequency count.

questions.prompt: In a sample of $150$ car speeds, $20\%$ of vehicles exceeded $V\text{ km/h}$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the cumulative percentage of vehicles travelling at or below $V\text{ km/h}$, and calculate the target cumulative frequency needed to find $V$ on the graph.

questions.prompt: A cumulative frequency curve represents the journey times (in minutes) of $180$ train commuters. The curve passes through the coordinates $(15, 24)$, $(25, 63)$, $(40, 135)$, and $(60, 180)$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the number of commuters whose journey time is at most $25$ minutes, and the number whose journey time exceeds $40$ minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the number of commuters with journey times between $15$ and $40$ minutes, and find what fraction of the total sample this represents in simplest form.

questions.prompt:
The daily sales revenues (in hundreds of dollars) for $120$ shops are summarized by a cumulative frequency graph. The curve gives the following readings:
$$\text{At } CF = 30,\; x = 18;\quad \text{at } CF = 60,\; x = 27;\quad \text{at } CF = 90,\; x = 38$$

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the median sales revenue and the lower quartile in hundreds of dollars.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State the upper quartile $Q_3$, calculate the interquartile range (IQR), and state the range of revenue in dollars representing the middle $50\%$ of shops.

questions.prompt: A cumulative frequency curve displays the heights (in cm) of $150$ plants. Readings from the curve show that $CF = 45$ at $18\text{ cm}$ and $CF = 120$ at $32\text{ cm}$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the 30th percentile of plant heights, and state the percentage of plants taller than $32\text{ cm}$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The 80th percentile is estimated at $32\text{ cm}$. If the top $10\%$ of plants are classified as 'tall', state the target cumulative frequency for the minimum height of a 'tall' plant, and explain why this height must exceed $32\text{ cm}$.

questions.prompt: The scores $S$ of $200$ applicants in an aptitude test are represented by a cumulative frequency curve that passes through the consecutive points $(40, 30)$, $(60, 90)$, $(80, 160)$, and $(100, 200)$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using linear interpolation, estimate the lower quartile $Q_1$ and the median score of the applicants.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using linear interpolation between $(60, 90)$ and $(80, 160)$, estimate the number of applicants who scored at most $75$ marks, and find the percentage of applicants who scored greater than $75$ marks.

questions.prompt: A cumulative frequency graph for the masses $m$ (in kg) of $160$ adult sheep gives quartiles $Q_1 = 48.0\text{ kg}$, $\text{Median} = 56.5\text{ kg}$, and $Q_3 = 63.5\text{ kg}$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the interquartile range of the sheep masses, and calculate the semi-interquartile range (quartile deviation).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: An animal is considered unusually light if its mass is below $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, and unusually heavy if its mass exceeds $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$. Calculate the lower and upper outlier boundaries for this dataset.

questions.prompt:
The reaction times $t$ (in milliseconds) of $240$ participants are summarized by a cumulative frequency curve. The curve passes through the coordinates:
$$(150, 0),\; (200, 36),\; (250, 108),\; (300, 186),\; (360, 222),\; (440, 240)$$

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the minimum recorded reaction time in the distribution, and find the number of participants with reaction times between $200\text{ ms}$ and $360\text{ ms}$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using linear interpolation between the given coordinates, estimate the lower quartile $Q_1$ and the upper quartile $Q_3$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A participant qualifies for an advanced reflex task if their reaction time is among the fastest $15\%$ of all participants. Estimate the maximum qualifying reaction time to the nearest millisecond.

questions.prompt:
The weekly household expenditure on groceries $E$ (in dollars) for $300$ families is represented by a cumulative frequency curve. The curve passes through the coordinates:
$$(60, 0),\; (100, 45),\; (140, 120),\; (180, 225),\; (220, 276),\; (280, 300)$$

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using linear interpolation, estimate the median expenditure and the 90th percentile of expenditure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using linear interpolation, estimate the interquartile range (IQR) of weekly grocery expenditures.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Families spending more than 200 dollars per week are eligible for a luxury food survey. Using linear interpolation between $(180, 225)$ and $(220, 276)$, estimate the number of families eligible for the survey, and find the probability that a randomly chosen family spends between 120 and 200 dollars.
